newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to announce deal seeking to end sweatshops.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to announce deal seeking to end sweatshops.

text.p: President Bill Clinton plans to announce details on Monday of an agreement aimed at ending sweatshop conditions in apparel factories that U.S. companies use around the globe.

The agreement was the product of a presidential task force made up of U.S. clothing makers like Nike Inc, L.L. Bean, and Liz Claiborne Inc, labor unions and human rights groups which banded together to recommend steps to ensure products were not made under exploitative conditions.
"It is a truly historic and groundbreaking accomplishment," said a White House official who asked to remain unidentified.

White House officials would not confirm details of the agreement, but other sources involved in the deal said it would include a code of conduct on wages and working conditions, including a maximum 60-hour work week and a mechanism for inspecting apparel factories worldwide.

It was also believed to demand that factories not use workers under the age of 15, and companies that comply would be able to put a label on their clothing to assure consumers that the items were not made under sweatshop conditions.

The initiative came about after talk show host Kathie Lee Gifford, who lends her name to a line of clothing, was severely criticized last year for labor practices of factories making products under her name.
Some human rights groups were already criticizing details of the agreement before it was announced.

The San Francisco-based Global Exchange group, which said it had a copy of the agreement, attacked what it called the sanctioning of excessive overtime, the absence of a specific wage requirement and a provision for accounting firms rather than human rights groups monitoring labor practices.

"Now Nike can still pay its Vietnamese workers 20 cents an hour, push them to do countless hours of 'voluntary overtime,' use as its 'independent monitor' the accounting firm Ernst and Young that has no sensitivity toward workers, and be rewarded for this behavior with a 'no sweatshop' label. It doesn't make any sense," said a Global Exchange spokesman, Medea Benjamin.
But Michael Posner, executive director of the Lawyer's Committee for Human Rights, which was part of the task force, defended the agreement, calling it "an important first step."
"What we've done in some respects is to compromise between very different positions around the table," he said.
